pests.name: Stalk borer
pests.note_beginner: A caterpillar (the larva of a moth) that tunnels inside the stems. You may see a small hole in a stem and the top of that stem wilting and dying. Cut the affected stem off an inch or two below the hole, and clean up weeds and old stalks in fall, since the eggs overwinter in weedy debris.
pests.note_seasoned: The stalk borer (Papaipema nebris) bores into and tunnels up and down inside the stems; the top of an infested stem wilts and dies. Cut and destroy affected stems below the entry hole, and reduce overwintering eggs by clearing weeds and old stalks at season's end.

pests.name: Spider mites
pests.note_beginner: Very tiny pests that show up in hot, dry conditions. Leaves get pale yellow speckles and may have fine webbing, and drought-stressed plants are hit worst. Keep plants watered and spray the undersides of leaves with water or insecticidal soap.
pests.note_seasoned: Twospotted spider mites (Tetranychus urticae) feed on leaf undersides, which turn light yellow, with fine webbing in hot, dry spells; drought-stressed plants are most vulnerable. Keep soil moisture even and treat with insecticidal soap or ultrafine horticultural oil at 7 to 10 day intervals, and preserve predatory mites.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.note_beginner: Small soft insects that cluster on new growth. A strong spray of water or insecticidal soap handles them, and the many beneficial insects bee balm attracts often keep them in check.
pests.note_seasoned: Aphids (including Aphis monardae) cluster on tender growth; they are usually minor and held in check by the predators bee balm's flowers recruit. Hose off or treat with insecticidal soap or ultrafine horticultural oil if populations build.

diseases.name: Powdery mildew
diseases.note_beginner: The signature bee balm problem: a white, powdery coating on leaves and stems, common in humid weather and crowded plantings. Prevent it by planting in full sun, spacing plants for airflow, keeping the soil moist, watering the soil not the leaves, dividing every 2 to 3 years, and choosing resistant types like 'Jacob Cline' or 'Marshall's Delight'.
diseases.note_seasoned: The defining bee balm foliar disease (Erysiphe / Golovinomyces spp.), favored by humidity, crowding, and drought stress. Management is cultural and varietal: full sun, generous spacing and division for airflow, even soil moisture, base watering, fall sanitation of infected debris, and mildew-resistant cultivars ('Jacob Cline', 'Marshall's Delight', 'Raspberry Wine', the Balmy series). Do not compost infected debris.

diseases.name: Rust
diseases.note_beginner: Orange to brown powdery spots on the undersides of leaves, an occasional problem worse in damp, crowded conditions. Space plants for airflow, water at the base, and remove badly affected leaves.
diseases.note_seasoned: Rust (Puccinia spp.) shows as orange to brown pustules on leaf undersides, an occasional problem favored by leaf wetness and crowding. Manage with spacing, base watering, and sanitation of infected foliage; the same airflow and division practices that limit powdery mildew reduce it.
